newsitem.title: UK: BSE largest farm crisis ever to hit N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: BSE largest farm crisis ever to hit N.Ireland.

text.p: Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) was the biggest crisis to hit Northern Ireland's agricultural industry since the foundation of the province, a survey by accountants Coopers & Lybrand said on Tuesday.
The majority of those surveyed said the British government was responsible for the BSE crisis.
"Although we expected to find a serious downturn, the scale of the impact of BSE on all sections of agriculture is very depressing," Coopers & Lybrand chief economist Philip McDonagh said.
He said 97 percent of those surveyed believe Northern Ireland will never recover from the effects of BSE.

Coopers surveyed 60 chief executives and financial directors from Northern Ireland's leading agribusinesses. The annual average turnover of the companies surveyed was 11 million pounds ($18.27 million) and the firms collectively employ 2,165 people.
McDonagh said if the export ban, which was imposed on British beef during the BSE crisis, continues throughout 1997, more jobs will be lost and some businesses will go to the wall.
Almost every company (97 per cent) claimed to have been hit by BSE, with 70 per cent reporting a reduction in demand and one-in-five reporting cashflow problems.

On average, companies had experienced a fall of more that 22 percent in the value of orders over the last 12 months, Coopers said. More than 80 percent said BSE was the sole reason for reduced order levels.

Falling sales hit employment, with 23 percent of firms reporting job losses in 1996. A further seven percent expect more jobs to go in 1997, McDonagh said. He said potential job losses represent 8.0 percent of total employment in the 60 companies surveyed.

Three-quarters of those surveyed said BSE would continue to affect their trading activities during 1997, while 35 percent said that BSE will remain the single main factor influencing their business performance for the next year.

"A continuation of the export ban for another year would force the closure of about 8.0 percent of the firms surveyed," McDonagh said. "Just under 60 percent said another year of the ban would mean more cutbacks and further job losses."
A quarter of all the businesses surveyed expect to come under pressure from creditors or their banks if the export ban continues until the end of 1997. ($1=.6021 Pound)
